newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Hanbo founder summoned over loan scandal.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Hanbo founder summoned over loan scandal.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors on Thursday summoned the founder of the Hanbo Group over a loan scandal surrounding the conglomerate's failed steelmaking unit.
"We asked Mr Chung Tae-soo to report to the prosecution office by 3:00 p.m. (0600 GMT) today," a prosecutor involved in the probe into Hanbo said.

The prosecutors have already questioned top aides to Chung on how billions of dollars of loans were funnelled to Hanbo Steel Co, flagship of South Korea's 14th-largest conglomerate, or chaebol, to finance a massive steel mill.
Hanbo Steel, the country's second-largest steelmaker, filed for court receivership on Tuesday after piling up five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans from 61 banks and financial institutions.
The state banking watchdog on Wednesday opened a special probe into the main creditor banks of Hanbo Steel, which defaulted on debt repayments last week.
The Office of Bank Supervision said the probe into four leading commercial banks and a state-run bank would focus on whether they violated regulations in offering loans to Hanbo.
The five banks are Korea First Bank, Cho Hung Bank, Korea Exchange Bank, SEOULBANK and the state-run Korea Development Bank.

Opposition parties, calling the case the biggest financial scandal in the country's history, have accused the government of peddling influence to pressure creditor banks into offering loans to Hanbo without adequate collateral.
President Kim Young-sam on Monday ordered a probe into the Hanbo case, which has tainted his anti-corruption drive ahead of presidential elections in December.

After coming to power in 1993 on an anti-graft ticket, Kim promised to end one of the main legacies of past military-backed governments by severing the corrupt alliance betweeen politics and business.

Chung is one of the leading patriachs of South Korea's family-run conglomerates, which dominate the economy. Personal rivalries between chaebol heads have fuelled a drive by their companies into diverse business areas.
Banks have often been unwilling backers of reckless expansion, forced to extend loans by governments that have treated them as state cashiers.
